title: Slate on an Older Houston House
description: Slate can outlast the house if the copper and the nails are sound. Walking it like asphalt breaks pieces you cannot hide from the street.
html:
Slate on an older Houston house is usually the original roof, or close to it. The pieces can still be sound while the nails, the valley copper, and the flashing have given up. The mistake is treating it like a shingle roof: walking the field, nailing patches, and wondering why the street face looks chewed up.

Repair is a hook, not a nail through the face

A broken slate comes out. A new one goes in with a copper hook or a nailed strip hidden by the course above, so the face of the slate is not pierced. Copper nails are the fastener. Steel nails rust, swell, and pop the piece. We carry the traffic on ladders and hooks, replace what we break, and we do not send a crew across the field in ordinary boots.

The leak is often the valley or the dormer, not the slate you can see from the curb. Copper valleys crack at the fold after decades of heat. Chimney flashing pulls out of the mortar. Those are repairs. A field of slate that is delaminating, soft, or shedding in sheets is a different conversation. At that point you are choosing another slate roof, which is heavy and wants a deck and a frame that can carry it, or a lighter system.

When the weight is the decision

New slate is a structural question before it is a style question. If the frame was sized for the original and the original is staying, repairs keep the look. If the frame is tired, stone-coated steel can keep a textured profile without asking the rafters to hold quarried stone again. We will say which one the house is. We will not talk you into tearing off slate that still has decades in it.

If pieces are on the ground after a storm, leave the walking to someone who has slate hooks on the truck. Call (281) 541-0027 or request a free inspection. We will tell you whether it is a hook-in repair or a roof that is actually finished.
